At the end of our street stood a shop that repaired things nobody knew were broken.

Its window contained a brass telescope, three empty picture frames, a shoe with a bird’s nest in it, and a sign:

**PLEASE BRING ALL THE PIECES.**

I passed it every morning on my way to work. Every evening, too, though by then the window reflected the traffic and I mostly saw myself.

One Thursday, my kettle stopped boiling.

This was the sort of problem I understood. There would be a fuse, a wire, a small component with a name. I put the kettle in a shopping bag and went to the shop.

A bell rang when I opened the door, then rang again after I had closed it, as though reconsidering.

Behind the counter sat a woman knitting something long and gray. The room smelled of sawdust and oranges.

“What seems to be the trouble?” she asked.

“It won’t boil.”

“That is certainly a trouble.”

She took the kettle out of the bag, plugged it in, and flicked the switch. Nothing happened.

“Could be the element,” I said.

“Could be.”

She opened a drawer, selected a tiny screwdriver, and removed the base. I watched her set each screw in a saucer.

“When did it last work?”

“Yesterday.”

“And what were you doing?”

“Making tea.”

She looked up.

“Before that?”

I thought. “Talking to my mother.”

“Ah.”

“My mother lives in Bristol.”

“That doesn’t rule anything out.”

She peered into the kettle’s underside.

“You ended the call quickly.”

“I had things to do.”

“Of course.”

“She calls at inconvenient times.”

“Most people do.”

The woman reached in with tweezers and pulled out a small blue thread. It kept coming: six inches, a foot, a yard. She wound it around her finger.

“What is that?”

“Something caught in the mechanism.”

“It’s an electric kettle.”

“Yes,” she said. “They’re surprisingly vulnerable.”

When she finished, she had a blue ball of thread the size of a plum. She placed it beside the screws and fitted the base back on.

The kettle began to hiss.

“How much?”

“Call your mother.”

“I mean for the repair.”

“So do I.”

***

I didn’t call that night.

Instead I inspected the kettle, turning it upside down under the kitchen light. There was a scratch near the switch that I couldn’t remember seeing before. I wondered whether she had simply cleaned a contact.

On Friday morning I called my mother while the water boiled.

She told me the fox had returned to her garden. She told me someone had stolen a planter from outside the library. She asked whether I was eating properly.

I said yes.

There was a pause.

“What?” I asked.

“Nothing. I’m pleased you called.”

I leaned against the counter. The kettle clicked off. Neither of us said anything for a little while, and then she asked if I remembered the blue coat I had worn to school.

“The one with the enormous buttons?”

“You insisted on sleeping in it.”

“I don’t remember that.”

“You were very determined.”

Afterward, I made tea with water that had already begun to cool.

***

The following week I brought the woman a wristwatch.

It kept excellent time, but I hated looking at it.

She turned it over in her palm.

“A gift?”

“From my father.”

“Is he alive?”

“Yes.”

“Then this should be straightforward.”

It wasn’t. She worked for nearly an hour, using tools so small I could barely see them. Finally she loosened something beneath the face, and a dry seed fell onto the counter.

“An apology,” she said.

“His or mine?”

She slid it toward me.

“I can’t tell from here.”

I carried it home in my wallet. For three days I took it out whenever I paid for something, then tucked it behind a receipt.

On Sunday I called my father.

We discussed football, then his car, then the weather. I nearly hung up.

“I shouldn’t have said that at Christmas,” I told him.

“No,” he said.

I waited.

“Neither should I.”

After the call, I looked for the seed. It was still there. I planted it in a pot on the kitchen windowsill.

***

By autumn, the shop had become popular.

People queued with lamps, umbrellas, jammed drawers, music boxes. A man brought a door still attached to its frame. Two sisters arrived carrying opposite ends of a dining table.

There were complaints.

One customer wanted a refund because his repaired radio played only songs he had once loved. Another accused the woman of ruining a perfectly good mirror.

“What did you do to it?” I asked.

“Removed a flattering distortion.”

“Can you put it back?”

“Certainly.”

“Will you?”

“If she asks again.”

The woman never advertised. She closed for lunch. Sometimes she refused a job without explaining why.

***

In November, I found her packing.

The telescope was wrapped in newspaper. The empty frames were stacked by the door. She had finished the gray knitting; it was a scarf, much shorter than I expected.

“Are you leaving?”

“My sister has room for me.”

“What about the shop?”

“Someone will rent it.”

I stood there holding a toaster. It had been burning everything for a week.

She took it from me.

“This one really does need a new thermostat.”

“Oh.”

“I’ll order it before I go.”

Behind her, the window looked bare. Without the objects, I could see straight through to the street.

“I thought you might stay,” I said.

“I know.”

She wrote my name on a label and tied it to the cord.

***

A bakery opened there in February.

For a while, I resented it. Then one wet morning I went inside and bought two buns, still warm from the oven.

I took them to my father’s house.

We ate at the kitchen table. He wore his old cardigan, the one missing a button. I noticed it while he was telling me about a train journey.

This time I listened to the end.

Then I asked if he had a sewing kit.
